fig_003.caption: Figure 3. Phase-specific processing and in-pipeline publication workflow of PhenoPhaseR (Möller and Gerstmann, 2026). fig_004.caption: Figure 4. Quantitative characterisation of the winter wheat ( Triticum aestivum , DWD Plant ID 202) dataset, 1993-2025. (a) Out-of-sample mean absolute error (MAE) per year for all seven modelled phases; the heading phase (18) is highlighted. (b) For the heading phase, the number of contributing station observations (blue, left axis) declines by about 70 % over the period while the out-of-sample MAE (red, right axis) remains stable. (c) Median and interquartile range of the per-pixel Bayesian posterior standard error (BSE) of the heading interpolation, which increases as the network thins. (d) Cross-validated coverage assessment for heading: prediction-interval coverage probability (PICP, blue, left axis) against the nominal 0.90 level, and mean prediction-interval width (MPIW, grey, right axis), from separate five-fold crossvalidation. The quantities shown in all panels were derived from the VAM , GEM , and PIC tables of the winter wheat deposit (Möller et al., 2026b). fig_005.caption: Figure 5. The black outline marks the Uckermark district, for which the phenological window in Fig. 6 is extracted.

fig_006.caption: Figure 6. Extraction of a phenological window and its propagated uncertainty for winter wheat over the Uckermark district (outlined in Fig. 5), 1993-2025, following the window-extraction approach of PhenoWin (Möller et al., 2020). The interpolated entry dates of shooting (15) and heading (18) (points) and the intervening window are shown with BSE-based uncertainty bands derived from the per-pixel modelmean precision; dashed lines give the linear trends of the two entry dates, with the fitted equations annotated.

fig_007.caption: Figure 7. Derivation of the phase-resolved weather indicator for the Uckermark district in 2018, mirroring Fig. 8 of Möller et al. (2019): (a) Germany-wide E-OBS daily precipitation for the wettest day of the shooting-heading window, with the district outlined; (b) daily precipitation (bars, spatial mean over the district) during the window, with whiskers spanning the ± 1 σ E-OBS ensemble spread of each day, overlaid with the accumulated indicator WI (line). Orange bands at the two phase boundaries span ± 1 BSE and visualise the BSE-based phenological sensitivity component; the blue ribbon around the accumulated indicator spans its ± 1 σ precipitation component, obtained by accumulating the daily spread in quadrature. The dotted vertical marks the day mapped in (a). For 2018 the window spans DOY 113 ± 1 . 5 to DOY 143 ± 1 . 0 , yielding WI =16 . 3 ± 2 . 3 mm(precipitation component).

fig_008.caption: Figure 8. Germany-wide weather indicator (WI, cumulative precipitation during the winter wheat shooting-heading window) and its approximate uncertainty decomposition for 2018 on the E-OBS 0.1 ◦ grid. Top row : the indicator and the absolute 1 σ contributions of the phenological component ( u pheno , propagated PHASE BSE), the precipitation component ( u precip , accumulated E-OBS ensemble spread), and their quadrature total. Bottom row : the corresponding relative uncertainties ( σ/WI ) for cells with WI ≥ 10 mm, with the WI panel repeated for reference. The σ scales are capped at 30 mm and 30 %, with a 10-class quantile colour classification; the yellow outline marks the Uckermark district of Figs. 5-6.

fig_009.caption: Figure 9. Weather indicator and approximate two-component uncertainty for the Uckermark district, 1993-2025. Top : median WI over the district's E-OBS cells with the propagated ± 1 σ band (dark) and the spatial interquartile range across cells (light). Middle : stacked absolute 1 σ contributions of the phenological (PHASE BSE, orange) and precipitation (E-OBS ensemble spread, blue) components. Bottom : the same contributions relative to the indicator ( σ/WI , stacked) for years with WI ≥ 10 mm; dashed lines mark illustrative relative-uncertainty levels of 15 % and 25 %. The lines are shown as visual reference levels and do not represent formal suitability thresholds for a specific application.

metric_candidate_hints.excerpt:
Abstract. Spatially and temporally consistent information on crop development is needed for many agro-environmental applications. In Germany, the volunteer phenology network of the German Meteorological Service (Deutscher Wetterdienst, DWD) provides long-term observations of crop development. However, the observations are irregularly distributed and contain spatial and temporal gaps. In this study, we present a Germany-wide, gridded time series of interpolated phenological phase-entry dates for eight major crop types. The dataset was produced with the open-source PhenoPhaseR workflow, which implements the PHASE approach and combines a photoperiod-weighted growing-degree-days model with a spatial generalised additive model. The data are provided at 1 km resolution in ETRS89/UTM zone 32N (EPSG:25832) for 1993-2025; spring barley is available for 2014-2025. For each crop and phase, the phase-entry day-of-year (DOY) is stored as a multi-band Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFF with one band per year. Each phase-year surface is evaluated using held-out observations, while predictioninterval coverage is assessed separately by five-fold cross-validation. metric_candidate_hints.source_section: 3.3.4 Spatially explicit uncertainty and prediction-interval coverage
metric_candidate_hints.excerpt: Alongside each DOY surface we provide a per-pixel uncertainty layer (BSE), the Bayesian posterior standard error of the fitted mean returned by the spatial model. BSE is a model-internal statistical uncertainty - the model's own estimate of the precision of its fitted surface - and not a validated predictive uncertainty. It generally increases where the fitted surface is less constrained by observations and decreases where observations are denser (Sect. 2.3.5). Spatial summaries of the BSE field (percentiles per phase and year) are tabulated in the GEM files. For the heading phase, the median per-pixel BSE rises from 0.76 days in 1993 to 1.38 days in 2025 (Fig. 4c), tracking the decline of the observation network shown in Fig. 4b and illustrating how the layer flags the years and regions in which the interpolated surface is least constrained.

metric_candidate_hints.source_section: 3.3.4 Spatially explicit uncertainty and prediction-interval coverage
metric_candidate_hints.excerpt: To assess predictive coverage separately from the BSE, we additionally report the prediction-interval coverage probability (PICP) and the mean prediction-interval width (MPIW) at a nominal 90 % level (PIC files), following the reliability-sharpness protocol for validating predictive uncertainty (Schmidinger and Heuvelink, 2023). These metrics are obtained from a separate five-fold cross-validation in which each station is held out exactly once. The prediction interval combines the fold-specific BAMmodel-mean standard error with the residual variance of the final production model. For the heading phase, the observed coverage is close to nominal throughout, with a mean PICP of 0.900 (range 0.888-0.920 across years) and a mean interval width of 16.0 days (range 12.6-21.4 days; Fig. 4d). The nominal 90 % intervals therefore show close-to-nominal empirical coverage even in the most recent, sparsely observed years, where the intervals widen (larger MPIW) without a clear loss of coverage. By reporting BSE and the cross-validated coverage assessment separately, the user receives both the model-internal precision estimate and information on how well the nominal prediction intervals perform within the validation framework.

metric_candidate_focus.source_section: 3.3.4 Spatially explicit uncertainty and prediction-interval coverage
metric_candidate_focus.excerpt: To assess predictive coverage separately from the BSE, we additionally report the prediction-interval coverage probability (PICP) and the mean prediction-interval width (MPIW) at a nominal 90 % level (PIC files), following the reliability-sharpness protocol for validating predictive uncertainty (Schmidinger and Heuvelink, 2023). These metrics are obtained from a separate five-fold cross-validation in which each station is held out exactly once. The prediction interval combines the fold-specific BAMmodel-mean standard error with the residual variance of the final production model. For the heading phase, the observed coverage is close to nominal throughout, with a mean PICP of 0.900 (range 0.888-0.920 across years) and a mean interval width of 16.0 days (range 12.6-21.4 days; Fig. 4d). The nominal 90 % intervals therefore show close-to-nominal empirical coverage even in the most recent, sparsely observed years, where the intervals widen (larger MPIW) without a clear loss of coverage. By reporting BSE and the cross-validated coverage assessment separately, the user receives both the model-internal precision estimate and information on how well the nominal prediction intervals perform within the validation framework.

Only DWD crop-phase combinations that can be modelled with a sufficient number of suitable observations are included in the dataset (Table 2). Station density also varies considerably over space and time. Predictions in sparsely observed regions should therefore be treated with greater caution, particularly where they extend beyond the main support of the observation network (cf. Meyer and Pebesma, 2021).
Regardless of the station, the gridded predictions cover the complete territory of Germany and are not masked by the actual occurrence of the respective crop or by agricultural land use. The raster values should therefore be interpreted as conditional phase-entry dates, i.e. the dates predicted if the respective crop were present at a grid cell. They do not indicate crop occurrence or cultivation suitability. The validation and the PICP/MPIW assessment are based on phenological observation locations and therefore assess model performance where observations of the respective crop are available, not across all cells of the Germany-wide prediction grid.

The BSE describes the model-internal precision of the fitted mean and does not represent total predictive uncertainty. In particular, the critical DOYs used for spatial interpolation depend on the gridded daily mean temperature input (Sect. 2.2), while uncertainty in this temperature grid is not propagated into the BSE. The held-out accuracy metrics reflect the combined effect of the modelling steps when predictions are compared with observed entry dates, but the published per-pixel BSE should be interpreted as a measure of model-mean precision.

The 75/25 validation is conditional on the preceding filtering and thermal-time quantile selection. The adaptive filter variant and the MAE-optimal thermal-time quantile are determined before the spatial validation split. The reported errors therefore describe the performance for the retained observations and may be optimistic compared with the unfiltered volunteer record. In addition, phenological entry dates are spatially autocorrelated and the DWD volunteer network is not a probability sample. Randomly held-out stations can therefore remain spatially dependent on training stations. The global validation metrics should consequently be interpreted together with the spatial BSE and station-density information.

The five-fold PICP/MPIW assessment is out-of-sample with respect to the spatial BAM fit, but remains conditional on the preceding filtering and thermal-time selection. In addition, the interval widths use the residual variance of the final all-data production model. The PICP/MPIW statistics should therefore be interpreted as a cross-validated coverage assessment of the published modelling framework rather than as a fully nested independent validation.

The uncertainty propagation in the weather-indicator use case is an illustrative approximation. The phenological component is based on ± 1 BSE shifts and therefore represents sensitivity to model-mean precision rather than a calibrated phenological prediction interval. The quadrature accumulation of the daily E-OBS ensemble spread assumes independent daily errors, while aggregation of the 1 km BSE to the coarser E-OBS grid does not explicitly account for spatial covariance. The resulting u total should therefore be interpreted as a transparent two-component uncertainty estimate rather than as a complete predictive uncertainty budget.
Despite these limitations, the dataset combines long-term coverage, documented validation, spatially explicit quality information and reproducible data publication. The accompanying quality information allows users to assess the suitability of individual crop-phase-year combinations for regional and Germany-wide applications.
